fatal_errors: The hypothesis addresses hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 under tensile and fracture testing, whereas the target concerns composition screening and room-temperature compression of as-cast Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W alloys.
It omits the target intervention: validation of rule-of-mixtures modulus estimates, screening of 38,326 compositions using modulus, VEC, and density, and selection of Nb15Mo2.5Ta40V40W2.5.
It replaces the target VEC–dislocation-mobility mechanism with an unsubstantiated DIC/active-learning crack model.
The claimed 10% accuracy and 70% computational reduction have no support in the cited evidence.

Neither citation validates DIC-calibrated mesoscale surrogates for predicting modulus, yield strength, or fracture toughness in this alloy; E1 concerns high-entropy ceramics and explicitly cautions that quantitative toughness measurements are unreliable.
The proposed benchmark risks calibration/test leakage and does not specify held-out microstructures, sample size, comparator implementations, confidence intervals, or a measured efficiency endpoint.
explanation: This is a conceptually testable alternative workflow, but it does not reconstruct the hidden study. The target used a simple composition-based high-throughput screen in the Nb-Mo-Ta-V-W system and experimentally demonstrated that lowering VEC while retaining modulus transformed compressive fracture strain from about 2% to 35.7 ± 0.9%, with yield strength of 1115 ± 18 MPa. The generated hypothesis instead invents a DIC–active-learning framework for a different alloy, loading mode, and property objective. Its stated boundaries are reasonable in generic terms, and the citations support only broad claims that atomistic methods can be expensive and fracture resistance is difficult to quantify. They do not substantiate the proposed mechanism or numerical gains. A decisive benchmark would require preregistered, fully held-out specimens and microstructures, fixed model weights before unblinding, valid standardized toughness geometry, explicit legacy-method comparators, and separate pass/fail criteria for predictive error and wall-clock or compute-cost reduction.
